item.title: How to type refs in React with TypeScript
item.description: Managing DOM elements or keeping mutable values between renders in React requires the useRef hook, but doing it correctly in TypeScript can be tricky for many developers. As the creator of CoreUI, I’ve implemented thousands of components where precise type definitions for refs were critical for stability. The most efficient and modern way to type refs is by using TypeScript generics to specify the exact DOM element or value type the ref will hold. This approach eliminates the need for type assertions and ensures that your IDE provides accurate autocompletion and error checking.

item.title: How to use refs to access DOM elements in React
item.description: Using refs to access DOM elements enables direct manipulation when React’s declarative paradigm isn’t sufficient for specific use cases. As the creator of CoreUI, I’ve used refs extensively for integrating third-party libraries, managing focus, and implementing complex interactions. From my expertise, the most effective approach is using the useRef hook to create persistent references that survive component re-renders. This technique provides imperative access to DOM elements while maintaining React’s component lifecycle.

item.title: How to use useRef in React
item.description: Using useRef is essential for accessing DOM elements directly, storing mutable values, and integrating with third-party libraries in React applications. As the creator of CoreUI, a widely used open-source UI library, I’ve implemented useRef in countless React components for focus management, scroll positioning, and integrating with non-React libraries in enterprise applications. From my expertise, the most effective approach is to use useRef for DOM references and persistent value storage. This method provides direct DOM access without causing re-renders, making it perfect for imperative operations and performance-critical scenarios.
